artboards.title: How a second document type fits

annotations.text:
Today, drawn from the real stylesheets at 1440x900.
The yellow boxes are the three pane headers at their actual heights: 112 / 40 / 38 px. The results pane has no header at all, so the editor and the table just butt into each other.

A, with B's full-height inspector. Four cells on one 36 px band; four columns below it; a 26 px status bar.
The inspector is now a peer of the document column rather than a region inside the results pane. That is what lets the whole selection - five documents here - be readable at once, and it is also what lets it serve ANY document, not just query results.
The editor gives up the width it did not need: 734 px is about 85 columns of SQL.

The same shell with a table-inspection document in the middle. Nothing moved: the schema drawer, the band, the status bar and the inspector are untouched.
The document is the SAME two-surface anatomy as a SQL file - facts where the editor would be, an ordinary results table where the results would be - so the snapshot rows get selection, the anchor strip and the inspector for free. Here two snapshots are selected and their Iceberg summary maps are flattened into readable fields, which is exactly the case you cannot read in a cell.

Where the new document type touches the chrome: one hover button in the tree, one icon in the chip, one extra kind of row in Cmd+P, and a different chip menu. Everything else is the anatomy it already has.
Worth knowing before committing: this is a real change in State.svelte.ts - Workspace.files becomes a list of documents of more than one type, activeFile/activeResult assumptions in Application.svelte have to move, and persist() re-maps each field by hand, so a table document needs its own line there or it silently will not survive a reload.

The three states. Closed: the table has the whole pane. One cell: one document, one field. A block - rows deep by columns wide: one document per row, structs flattened to dotted paths, and a value that gets its own block. The strip under the table always carries the anchor cell in full, whatever its column width.
Drawn before the inspector went full height, so the panel here is the height of the results pane; the content and behaviour are unchanged.

Two text sizes, four heights, three radii, one icon size, one accent with four jobs. Every artboard is built from exactly this.
The column header keeps its two lines: name over type.

Kept for reference. B is where the full-height inspector came from; its card ground and warm palette are still on the table if you want the looser look. C is the one-global-bar option, and its collapsed 44 px inspector rail is still the cheapest way to hide the panel completely.
